claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! To get started, I need to ask you some questions about your child.

**First, let me ask about your child's age:**

The eligibility rules differ based on whether your child is:
- Under 16 years old
- Between 16 and 19 years old
- 20 or over

**How old is your child?** (Or if you have multiple children, let's start with one and we can assess each child.)

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm asking about my son Alex - he's 17 years old.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you're asking about your son Alex who is 17 years old.

Since Alex is between 16 and 19 years old, there are additional requirements to check. Let me navigate to the next step.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect. For young people aged 16-19 like Alex, Child Benefit can continue if they meet certain education or training requirements.

**I need to know: Is Alex currently in any of the following situations?**

1. **In approved education or training** (such as full-time non-advanced education at school or college, or approved training programs)

2. **Has recently left education or training** (within the last 20 weeks)

3. **Neither** - not in education/training and didn't recently leave

Which situation applies to Alex?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Alex is currently in education - he's studying for his A-levels at college.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Alex is studying for his A-levels at college, which is a form of education. Now I need to check if this education meets the specific requirements for Child Benefit eligibility.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! A-levels are specifically listed as an approved qualification for Child Benefit purposes. Now I need to verify a few more details about Alex's education to ensure it meets all the requirements:

**1. Is Alex's course full-time?** (This means at least 12 hours per week of supervised study - which typical A-level courses are)

**2. Is this education funded by an employer or linked to a job that an employer has agreed to provide in the future?** (This would typically not apply to regular A-level college courses)

**3. If Alex is married or in a civil partnership**, is he financially dependent on you? (If he's not married/in a civil partnership, we can skip this)

Let me know about these points so I can continue the assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Yes, it's a full-time course at college - he's there during the week with regular classes and study time.

No, it's not funded by an employer or anything like that - it's just regular college.

And no, Alex isn't married or in a civil partnership.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect! Alex's A-level course meets all the education requirements:
- ✓ A-levels are approved non-advanced education
- ✓ Full-time course (12+ hours per week)
- ✓ Not employer-funded
- ✓ Not married/in civil partnership

Let me move to the next check.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Excellent! Now I need to check Alex's work situation.

**Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week (or not in paid work at all)?**

This is important because young people aged 16+ who work 24 hours or more per week are not eligible for Child Benefit, even if they're in education.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Actually, Alex does work quite a bit - he has a part-time job at the local supermarket and works pretty much full-time hours there alongside his college course. I think it's around 24 hours or maybe a bit more per week.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I see. This is an important point. If Alex is working 24 hours or more per week, this affects his eligibility for Child Benefit, even though he's in approved education.

Let me ask for clarification: **Is Alex working 24 hours per week or more?** 

If it's exactly 24 hours or more, this would make him ineligible. If it's less than 24 hours per week, he would still qualify.

Do you know more precisely how many hours per week Alex works at the supermarket?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he definitely works 24 hours or more per week - it's a proper part-time job that he fits around his college schedule.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Thank you for confirming that. Unfortunately, this is a critical factor for eligibility.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I'm sorry to inform you that based on the information you've provided, **you are not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex**.

**Here's why:**

Even though Alex is 17 years old and studying A-levels (which is approved non-advanced education), the rules state that young people aged 16 or over who work 24 or more hours per week are not eligible for Child Benefit.

**Important guidance:**

- Child Benefit stops when a child aged 16 or over starts paid work for 24+ hours per week
- If Alex reduces his working hours to less than 24 hours per week while continuing his education, you may be able to claim Child Benefit again
- If his work situation changes, you can reapply

**Do you have any other children you'd like to check eligibility for?** If not, I can provide you with the final assessment.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text:
Oh, I see. That's disappointing, but thank you for explaining it clearly. No, Alex is my only child, so that's all I needed to check.

So just to confirm - even though he's still in full-time education doing his A-levels, because he works 24 hours or more per week, I can't claim Child Benefit for him?

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Yes, that's correct. I understand this is disappointing, but let me confirm the situation clearly:

**Even though Alex is:**
- ✓ 17 years old (within the 16-19 age range)
- ✓ In full-time approved education (A-levels)
- ✓ At a regular college course (not employer-funded)

**He is ineligible because:**
- ✗ He works 24 hours or more per week

The Child Benefit rules specifically state that young people aged 16 or over who work 24+ hours per week are not eligible, regardless of whether they're also in education.

**However, there is some flexibility:**
If Alex's work hours drop below 24 hours per week at any point while he continues his education, you could become eligible again and reapply for Child Benefit.

Let me now record this final assessment for you.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
**Final Assessment Complete**

**Result: INELIGIBLE for Child Benefit**

**Summary:**
- **Child:** Alex (age 17)
- **Status:** Ineligible

While Alex meets the education requirements by studying A-levels full-time at college, he does not meet the work requirements because he works 24 or more hours per week. The rules are clear that 16-19 year olds working at this level are not qualifying children for Child Benefit purposes.

**What you can do:**
- If Alex reduces his work hours to less than 24 hours per week while continuing his education, you can reapply for Child Benefit
- Keep this in mind if his circumstances change

If you have any questions about this decision or need further clarification, please feel free to ask!
